title: The Earring, the Owl, and the Pellet Date Published: June 3, 2026 Original URL: https://samanthalippert.substack.com
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Lippert describes how a scene in Avi's children's novel Poppy — a mouse wearing an earring being eaten by an owl, earring and all — spontaneously generated a genuine scientific question in her third-grade classroom: does the earring end up in the owl pellet? The article traces the journey from literary moment to scientific investigation: a student's quiet observation ('the earring went inside the owl') opened a door that Lippert chose to walk through rather than close, pivoting the lesson to actual owl pellet dissection. At the heart of her pedagogy is the argument that great literature and real science are not separate curriculum strands but that authentic fiction creates intellectual friction — wonder, shock, injustice — that becomes the motivation for scientific inquiry. Lippert describes the actual dissection process: students working in small groups with toothpicks and magnifying glasses, sorting bones by size and consulting identification charts to reconstruct the owl's meal from its compressed, tangled remains. The earring thread that runs through Poppy — dropped at Ragweed's death, coughed up in the pellet, found by Poppy, and worn as a memorial — functions as an emotional through-line that keeps student attention tied to the scientific question throughout. The article is both a classroom narrative and a quiet argument that the distinction between 'science time' and 'reading time' is a bureaucratic convenience, not a description of how curiosity and learning actually work.
points: The most powerful science motivation is not a teacher's introduction but a student's own question, and story is one of the most reliable generators of the emotional state — wonder, indignation, puzzlement — from which genuine scientific questions emerge.

Avi's narrative move of 'earring and all' does pedagogical work that a science textbook cannot replicate: it names something specific, memorable, and emotionally charged that creates a cognitive thread the student wants to resolve through investigation.

Lippert's decision to follow the student's question rather than redirect to the planned lesson is the key pedagogical move — not because curricula don't matter, but because the question arrived with intrinsic motivation attached, which is the rarest and most valuable resource in any classroom.

The owl pellet dissection as described is not a decorative activity but a genuine epistemic exercise: students encounter ambiguity (bones that don't clearly belong to a known animal), use reference tools to make inferences, and must accept that some questions remain open.

The Poppy example generalizes: virtually any novel with precise sensory detail about the natural world can generate authentic science questions — the teacher's craft is in noticing when a student's response to fiction has crossed from emotional to curious-and-investigative.
quotes: Down came his left claw. It was more successful, clamping around Ragweed's head and neck like a vise of needles, killing him instantly. The next moment the owl soared back into the air. A lifeless Ragweed — earring glittering in the moonlight — hung from a claw. As for the hazelnut, it fell to the earth like a cold stone.
Mr. Ocax returns to his watching tree and 'shifted the dead Ragweed from talon to beak in one gulp. The mouse disappeared down his throat, earring and all.' Earring and all. Page eight. Chapter one.

My class of third graders, sitting and staring at their books, don't make a sound for a full three seconds after I read that aloud. I can see them processing it — the injustice of it, the speed of it, the way the author describes those claws like grappling hooks and doesn't look away.
Then someone says, very quietly: 'The earring went inside the owl.' My students weren't just reacting to a story anymore. They were asking a science question.
She 'caught sight of something that glittered.' Ragweed's earring. Coughed up in a pellet. Right there in the pile at the bottom of Mr. Ocax's watching tree.

When Fiction Opens a Door: The story doesn't let us forget that earring. Later on, Poppy is forced to stand beneath Mr. Ocax's tree while her father begs for permission to move their family to a new home.
